questions.text: Which tool manages Rust versions and related tooling?
questions.explanation: `rustup` is described as the command-line tool for managing Rust versions and related tools.

questions.text: Which function is the first code executed in every Rust executable?
questions.explanation: The `main` function is identified as the first code that runs in every executable Rust program.

questions.text: What does the exclamation mark in `println!` indicate?

answers.text: It calls a macro rather than an ordinary function

questions.explanation: The material explains that `!` marks a macro invocation; without it, the syntax would look like a function call.

questions.text: Which command compiles a standalone `main.rs` file without Cargo?
questions.explanation: The example compiles the file with `rustc main.rs` before running it.

questions.text: What practical consequence follows from Rust being ahead-of-time compiled?

answers.text: The program normally has to be interpreted on every run
Compilation produces an executable that can run without the Rust compiler
Every Rust binary requires a JVM at runtime
Source code is compiled only when each function is called for the first time

questions.explanation: Rust compiles the program ahead of time into an executable; running the finished binary does not require the Rust compiler.

questions.text: What is Cargo's primary role in the Rust ecosystem?

answers.text: Building projects and managing their packages and dependencies
Compiling source code instead of `rustc` without using `rustc` internally

questions.explanation: Cargo is Rust's build system and package manager: it manages dependencies and coordinates project builds.

questions.text: Which command creates a new Cargo project named `hello_cargo`?
questions.explanation: The example creates the project with `cargo new hello_cargo`.

questions.text: Where does Cargo expect a project's source files?
questions.explanation: The material says Cargo expects source files inside the `src` directory.

questions.text: Which file is Cargo's TOML configuration file?
questions.explanation: `Cargo.toml` is described as Cargo's configuration file in TOML format.

questions.text: What is the `[dependencies]` section of `Cargo.toml` used for?
questions.explanation: The `[dependencies]` section starts the list of external packages on which the project depends.

questions.text: Where is the binary from a normal Cargo debug build placed?
questions.explanation: A normal build uses the debug profile, so Cargo places the binary in `target/debug`.

questions.text: What does `Cargo.lock` store?

answers.text: The exact versions of project dependencies

questions.explanation: `Cargo.lock` stores exact dependency versions and is used for reproducible builds.

questions.text: What does `cargo run` do?

answers.text: Compiles the project and runs the resulting binary
Only checks the code without producing a binary

questions.explanation: `cargo run` combines building and running the project in one command.

questions.text: What does `cargo check` do?

answers.text: Checks whether the code compiles without creating an executable
Updates every dependency beyond the Cargo.toml constraints

questions.explanation: `cargo check` quickly verifies that the code compiles while skipping creation of the executable.

questions.text: Which command creates an optimized release build?
questions.explanation: The material uses `cargo build --release` for the final optimized build.

questions.text: Why must the string passed to `std::io::Stdin::read_line` be provided through a mutable reference?

answers.text: `read_line` writes the input into the supplied `String`
Every `String` in Rust must be mutable
Immutable references cannot be passed to standard-library functions
`String::new()` returns an immutable reference that must be converted

questions.explanation: `read_line` appends user input to the supplied `String`, so it requires a `&mut String`.

source.locator: Chapter 2 — Programming a Guessing Game, pp. 25–27

questions.text: What does `std::io::Stdin::read_line` return when reading into a `String`?

answers.text: `std::io::Result<usize>`, where the `usize` is the number of bytes read
A bare `usize` with no way to report an error
`Option<String>` containing a copy of the input

questions.explanation: `read_line` mutates the supplied buffer and returns `io::Result<usize>`; on success the value is the number of bytes read.

source.locator: Chapter 2 — Programming a Guessing Game, pp. 27–28

questions.text: What does `expect` do when a `Result` contains `Err`?

answers.text: Terminates the program and prints the supplied message

questions.explanation: If the `Result` is `Err`, `expect` terminates the program and displays the supplied message.

source.locator: Chapter 2 — Programming a Guessing Game, pp. 28

questions.text: Which tasks does Cargo perform? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Automatically writing the program's business logic

questions.explanation: Cargo builds code, downloads dependencies, and builds them; it does not write business logic.

questions.text: Which information is specified in the `[package]` section of `Cargo.toml`? Select all correct answers.
questions.explanation: In the example, `[package]` contains `name`, `version`, and `edition`.

questions.text: Which statements are true about running `cargo run` again without making changes? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Cargo can detect that the files have not changed
Cargo can skip rebuilding the project
The already built binary is simply run
Cargo always deletes `target` and rebuilds everything

questions.explanation: The material shows that when nothing has changed, Cargo skips unnecessary rebuilding and runs the binary.

questions.text: How does `cargo check` differ from `cargo build`? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: `cargo check` verifies that the code compiles
`cargo check` does not create an executable
`cargo check` is often faster than `cargo build`

questions.explanation: `cargo check` skips binary code generation and is therefore often faster; `cargo build` creates an executable.

questions.text: Which properties are characteristic of a Cargo release build? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: It compiles faster than a debug build specifically because of the optimizations

questions.explanation: The release profile enables optimizations and places the binary in `target/release`, but optimizations increase compilation time.

questions.text: Which statements about `String::new()` are correct? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: It is an associated function of the `String` type
It creates a new empty string
The `::` syntax associates the function name with the `String` type
It reads a line from stdin by itself

questions.explanation: `String::new` is described as an associated function that creates an empty `String`; input is performed by a separate `read_line` call.

source.locator: Chapter 2 — Programming a Guessing Game, pp. 26

questions.text: Which statements about the external crate `rand` are correct? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: It is added to the `[dependencies]` section of Cargo.toml
Cargo downloads required dependencies from the registry associated with Crates.io
Cargo can also download `rand`'s own dependencies
In this section, `rand` is a built-in part of Rust's standard library

questions.explanation: The chapter emphasizes that random-number functionality here is not part of the standard library; `rand` is added as an external dependency, and Cargo also downloads its transitive dependencies.

source.locator: Chapter 2 — Programming a Guessing Game, pp. 30–31

questions.text: Which statements about reproducible builds with `Cargo.lock` are correct? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Cargo records the selected dependency versions in `Cargo.lock`
On later builds Cargo uses the recorded versions
This helps rebuild the same artifact with the same versions
`Cargo.lock` forces Cargo to ignore Cargo.toml constraints whenever an explicit update is requested

questions.explanation: The lock file records selected versions for later builds; an explicit update can change it within the declared specifications.

source.locator: Chapter 2 — Programming a Guessing Game, pp. 32

questions.text: Which actions does `cargo update` perform in the described scenario? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Ignores the currently locked versions in Cargo.lock while searching for an update
Finds the latest versions that satisfy the Cargo.toml requirements
Writes the selected versions back to Cargo.lock
Always moves to any later incompatible major/minor version regardless of Cargo.toml

questions.explanation: `cargo update` recalculates versions according to the `Cargo.toml` specifications and updates `Cargo.lock`; versions incompatible with the constraints are not selected automatically.

source.locator: Chapter 2 — Programming a Guessing Game, pp. 32–33
